claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr is treated as a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The relevant samples are bulk HfNbTaTiZr in oxygen-free and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen-containing states.
The predictive model will be calibrated using both defect-informed atomistic simulations and experimental conductivity measurements.
Model inputs will include temperature, defect-density indicators, oxygen content, and local structural descriptors.
The model can accurately predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr conductivity across 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The model can predict conductivity for HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Quantum and defect scattering dominate conductivity behavior in the 0–200 K regime.
Thermal vibrations and activated scattering processes become significant in the 300–1200 K regime.
Vacancy and interstitial densities, oxygen distribution, and local short-range order mediate conductivity behavior.
Explicit defect and oxygen descriptors allow the model to learn impurity- and defect-scattering effects.
Existing analytical conductivity models are based on perfect, defect-free crystals and neglect defect and impurity scattering.
Neglecting defect and impurity scattering causes significant deviations between analytical predictions and experiment in the specified temperature regimes.
The machine-learning model will match experimental conductivity more closely than the existing analytical models.
A proposed held-out benchmark is the 300 K conductivity of the approximately 1 wt.% oxygen specimen, illustrated by a measured value of about 1.2×10^6 S/m.
The prediction for the held-out 300 K benchmark should be within ±10% of the measured value.
Validated applicability is limited to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K and to oxygen levels near 0 and 1 wt.%.
Predictions for other temperature intervals or substantially different oxygen contents may be unreliable.
A benchmark prediction outside 1.08×10^6–1.32×10^6 S/m, assuming a measured value of 1.2×10^6 S/m, will falsify the stated accuracy criterion.
